Pat LaBarbera

Saxophonist Pat LaBarbera grew up in a musical family and went on to become a noteworthy soloist with the Buddy Rich Band, Elvin Jones, and as a leader of his own combo. He has also become a distinguished jazz educator in a number of Canadian universities.
Pat was interviewed via Zoom on January 5, 2021, by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.

My name is Monk Rowe for the Fillius Jazz Archive, and I’m very pleased to have Pat LaBarbera with me this afternoon. And we are in two different countries but we’re doing the Zoom thing. Welcome, Pat.
Thank you, Monk, thanks for having me.

Yeah. I wanted to tell you that I have been, as a child mostly, through Mount Morris many times. We used to travel from Rochester down to the Southern Tier to visit relatives. And when I saw that, about where you’re from and your brothers, and I wondered if the Mount Morris Shopper, which was the local newspaper, did they ever do a story on your family band?

Yeah, there was quite a — actually the Mount Morris Enterprise was the paper before that. There was two papers. You had the Picket Line Post and the Mount Morris Enterprise had early, really early stuff on us in the 50s. What the Shopper would do is they’d put those little photo sequences in. Like they’d put a picture from the past newspapers that were in town and then a little comment on that. But yes they did one on all of us and my father in that paper you know.
Were your mother and father both on the same page as far as, I don’t know if I can say “raising musicians” but I’m guessing this was not a chore for you.

Well no. I think my mother just went along with the program. She played piano and she was interested in music. My mother was a nurse. My father was the one that really got us going with it. And he started us off really and kind of grooming us as a family band, and then we would go out and play jobs with my father or with a kind of a composite of something that he had put together with the three of us. Then my mother got upset because she was left at home, so she started playing bass, learning how to play bass, and then we went out as a family band and worked as a family band.
So you were playing gigs at an early age. Did they pay you?

We used to get five dollars sometimes, which was pretty good in 1954, ’55 you know. But the jobs were like you played 55 minutes on and 5 minutes off, basically, for weddings. So I mean you were just going, going, going all the time. Yeah. I mean I © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-
started working in ’54 I think, ’54 yeah. I was eight. I was eight years old. And my brother Joe was probably working when he was around six or seven, maybe six.
What was the set list like at that time? You probably were playing Swing Era tunes but also maybe whatever was on the radio?

Swing and pop music of the day, Glenn Miller stocks, a lot of them were stock arrangements, a lot of Italian tunes. If it was Italian weddings we had to play all of the traditional Italian mazurkas and polkas. And so he had a whole library of that Italian music. And then the pop music of the day you know, which was in the 50s, and a lot of the stuff was — you had some funny stuff — but a lot of it was swing. He had quite a few stocks from the 30s and 40s basically, because he had his own dance band at one time so he had ordered all the stock arrangements. So you know we had “In the Mood” and “String of Pearls” and The Casa Loma Orchestra stuff, and you know he had bunches of books of jazz transcriptions, Frankie Trumbauer solo books, and Chu Berry solo books, and Toots Mondello books you know, so we had all of these transcribed solos that he would give us to read.
At some point did your father say, especially to you and John on trumpet, that, okay now it’s time to play music that’s not on the page, and how did he describe that?

I’ll tell you, my first experience with that, because we never did that. What happened was we always read the solos that were written in there. They were little note solos that were written. And the first time I remember we were playing a talent contest in Dansville, New York with the family band, I’ve even got a picture of the night somewhere where somebody took it from the audience. And I had to stand up and read the transcribed solo. And I looked down and I lost my place so I just started improvising. And after the set I remember we finished and I went offstage to my two brothers and I said, “Man, I just made up my own stuff and it felt really great.” I was really enthused about it. And that was the first time I ever had really improvised on my own. And then from then on, it didn’t last that long, the spark, I mean we kept doing it as kids. And it didn’t really kind of hit me until I got into high school that that’s the direction I wanted to go in. And it wasn’t my father, it was my school music teacher that really started the spark about jazz.
I see. Were you and your brothers, did you have some notoriety in high school like almost as if you were the quarterback and the wide receiver and the fullback or something on the football team?

No I mean we had some articles in the paper. We auditioned for the Ted Mack Amateur Hour, we auditioned for the Mickey Mouse Club, I remember that. And they put little articles on us in the paper, but it wasn’t really something that went anywhere or followed us anywhere. You know everybody knew that we played music and we were, they knew we were musicians. © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-
Where did you go to audition for the Mickey Mouse Club?

It was in Rochester, Sibley’s I think, it was at Sibley’s, that building upstairs on one of the floors. Jimmie Dodd came and he was one of the guys that auditioned us. And Steve Gadd of course went, I think Steve won, I think Steve won an audition. I remember Steve Gadd auditioned.
Wow. Was there any rivalry with your brothers regarding music?

No. We’ve always gotten along. We never had any kind of arguments that I can see. Basically I was the first one interested in jazz. I got interested in it, I roped my brother John and Joe into it, I got them into it, and then some local kids that were in school with us, I got one of them to play bass and a couple of them played trumpet. But we never really fought over anything. Even to this day we’re still in kind of an agreement. And it’s kind of unusual. You know I played a club here called The Rex and I know the club owner Bob is always amazed that the three brothers get along you know. But we’ve always gotten along.
I’m happy to hear that.
It was instilled, my father did that to us, just to make sure that none of us — I mean there was always little spats occasionally but never any grudges.
I see. What were your aspirations? You went to SUNY Potsdam. I had a SUNY experience at Fredonia. And I wonder, when you went there was your jazz interest met at SUNY Potsdam?

I have to say no, but I auditioned for Fredonia first. That’s where I wanted to go because I knew that Don Menza and Sam Noto — or Don Menza had gone there. And there’s a bass player named Linc Milliman who played bass — Linc was basically from six miles outside of Mount Morris is where he grew up, so I used to play with his father, his mother and his sisters and with Linc. And I knew they went to Fredonia so I auditioned for Fredonia but they turned me down because I couldn’t sight sing. You know they made me, like I played, an audition, and then they put a piece of sight singing up there and I never sang anything and so they turned me down. And then I went to Potsdam. See the other thing was that I wasn’t a clarinet player, I was a saxophone player and wanted to get into New York State as a saxophone player. But they didn’t take saxophone players. But the year that I went, in ’62, I was the first saxophone player in the State of New York that was allowed to go into the State of New York school system as just primarily a saxophone player. Because you always had to be a clarinet major and then double on saxophone player for what they had at that time called the “wind ensemble,” you probably remember William Musser had the wind ensemble. So when I went to Potsdam my music — you know at the time he did not want me there. He actually said, “How did you ever get into this school?” You know he was a clarinet major and you know he just © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

did not want me, made it difficult for me. And then there was an opening in the wind ensemble and Joe Roccisano, I don’t know if you know Joe, Joe was a great saxophone player. Joe was going to school at the time and he auditioned me on tenor to go into the wind ensemble, and he said, “Yeah, that’s good. You’ll pass. You can go in.” And my clarinet teacher balked and said, “No I don’t want him in the wind ensemble.” So with that animosity I only lasted one semester. And you know jazz was not — you know the school system at that time, the big band had to rehearse off campus. You couldn’t use the school facilities and all that. But yet they had sent a jazz combo from Potsdam to a Villanova festival and they got all kinds of notification, and a lot of these places got awards. I see Nick Brignola at Ithaca College with Reece Markowitz, they all got noticed and they won this award but yet you couldn’t practice jazz in the practice rooms at Ithaca College. It was a different era back then. Now Potsdam has a great jazz program. All of the schools do. Eastman does — at one time Eastman, you know, forget it.
Well if it’ll make you feel any better regarding Fredonia, Don Menza told me when he was at Fredonia he said practicing bebop was a felony, practicing Dixieland was just a misdemeanor.

Yeah I know Menza told stories about that. It was the turn of a different era of music. And I just happened to be right in the middle of that thing that was turning around in the 60s. And we’re talking 1962. I’m sure about ten years later everything had changed around because every school had to have some kind of big band or jazz band program.

Yeah I want to talk about that a bit later. I was reading in the Grove Dictionary of Jazz there’s an entry on you and your brothers. And I was going to read — you know it’s a challenge, they try to describe musicians’ styles, sometimes in one sentence for space reasons. And I was going to read what they said about you but I’m thinking how would you like an opportunity to describe your own playing and in about twenty words. Can you do that?

Well my playing comes from — the earliest references that I referenced were basically Gerry Mulligan, Prez, Stan Getz, Sonny Rollins, Coltrane. I mean I listened to all those guys. Lester Young was a huge influence on me and even to this day, I went through all the periods of music listening to everybody, studied with everybody that I could. And you know, playing with Elvin you had to play a certain way, or I felt that I did, or more modern, but even now today I go back to Lester Young and the things that I learned about Prez. So you know I’m drawn back to that. But I would say Stan Getz, Richie Kamuca, Lester Young for sure. I mean Prez, I copied a lot of Prez solos. And Gerry Mulligan was a huge influence on me, and all the guys that worked with Gerry Mulligan, because I bought all those albums, you know, “Ben Webster Meets Gerry Mulligan,” Johnny Hodges I used to copy Johnny Hodges’ solos. So all those guys were big influences. © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

Nice. Well I’ll read what they said. They should have called you. In regards to your style, “His style is derived principally from that of John Coltrane to which he adds his own rhythmic looseness and lyricism.

Yeah I mean you listen to early Trane and it’s Prez and it’s Gene Ammons and it’s Dexter you know. I mean they’re all in there. I mean everybody’s kind of mixed up in there. But I mean the time that I was probably being more recognized for my soloing would have been with Elvin Jones. With Buddy of course I was known as a soloist but with a big band you’re only going to get a small chunk of space to solo. Right? Maybe one big feature that you get that you know — the suite was something that I kind of inherited from Don Menza. And so with Elvin’s band, when they heard me play, and those articles were probably written back then, I was heavily into those by Trane. It’s pretty hard not to go down that road when you’re playing with Elvin, and then especially when you’re playing with Elvin and McCoy and Reggie Workman. All of the sudden there’s that trio behind you and, you know, I’m going to come out and play like Zoot Sims it just didn’t fit the flow of where I felt the time was. And I wanted to study and I learned that music. I used to go see Coltrane all the time when I was in Rochester or going to Berklee. That was one of the things you did. When he came to town you went down to see him.
Can you describe what that was like? Leaving the club after seeing Coltrane?

Well there was a couple of times when I left the club early and had to go outside just to kind of calm down because it was frantic, sometimes in that period we were catching him. ’64, ’65 ’66. It was just surely an eye opener and I learned, you know, the dedication. You used to watch Trane come off the bandstand and then go right into a room — either a room where they put the beer cases and all that, and he’d just keep playing. And then I was lucky enough when I was at Berklee one of my friends was a waiter at the Jazz Workshop. And he got us to go in, in the daytime we’d go in and listen to Trane practice. Because he would come to the Jazz Workshop, go into the dressing room, and then the three guys we would sit there and order a Coca Cola at lunch and there was nobody in the club and he would be practicing in the background and we’d be trying to figure out what he’s doing. And he’s right next to the bathroom so every once in a while we’d pretend we had to go to the bathroom and look in, and I remember seeing that he had a whole tableful of reeds and we used to just listen to see what he would be practicing.
I’m trying to form a question here about what did you try to copy?

Oh boy, Trane, I mean the sound was one of the things that I’ve always been drawn to. His use of vibrato in the later period, you know where he was almost into a classical vibrato. You know when I studied at Berklee with Joe Viola, he stressed classical etudes © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

but not playing in that style. And so what I was always listening to the way Trane would use his vibrato, where he would play — usually a jaw vibrato but sometimes a jaw and a diaphragm combination vibrato. I heard Sonny Rollins doing the same thing where they combine the flute — ha-ha-ha-ha-ha — with the ya-ya-ya-ya jaw, so you get two things working at once. You get the depth of the stomach vibrato — ha-ha-ha-ha — that’s going here and there. It’s kind of tricky. I just picked it up. But I mean I just copied a lot of his solos, not in total but like what was that phrase, and I would listen to what’s that idea. I would pick little devices out to see if there were things that I liked.
Did he ever go out too far, you know in his last year or so, for you to keep up with?

There were times when, you know like one of my, let’s see “Expression,” that album, there’s one there I really like from that period back and then forwards, the other ones like “Om” and some of those other ones — “Live in Seattle” there’s some things that I like. But there was a point where I decided I’m going to listen to all of that stuff and see what he’s trying to get across in there. You know I always studied it, being an educator also. I mean I always wanted to kind of understand what’s going on with him. Some of it I didn’t like all the time, but I always enjoyed the way he played. Not always the combination of instruments that he had, I could see he was searching for a certain thing. Everything didn’t appeal to me. But most of it did.
Okay. When you were at Berklee were you and your classmates sort of waiting for the phone call?

I wasn’t thinking that way when I first went there because when I came from Potsdam, well I didn’t come right there I ended up working for a year and did a lot of day jobs to save money to go to — to get the tuition because at the time Berklee was expensive — $500 a semester. A thousand dollars a year in 1962, that was unheard of.
It’s still unheard of.

My father had to go to some shady characters. I got enough, as much money as I could but my father tried to get a loan from the bank and they wouldn’t give it to them so he had to go to some other guys that he knew that were kind of under the radar. But he got the loan to get me to go to my first semester at Berklee. And then my other two brothers followed. John went to Potsdam and then cam to Berklee. Joe went directly to Berklee afterwards.
I see. They should have given him at least a discount for the family.
Right. Third one’s free.
But you know I’m sort of wondering, it seemed like Berklee was a place where bandleaders could go and pick up young musicians who were hungry to get out there and play. © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

Well you know in my first two years I didn’t think that way. I was just basically trying to learn everything I possibly could. We had bands, small bands, and Saturday morning, Sunday morning we’d be rehearsing with our own big bands that we put together. We had access to the practice rooms so we could put groups together. And there were a lot of guys that were in school at that time who later became big names. But we were all just trying to learn. By my third year, you see my problem was I made the mistake of every year going back to Mount Morris, New York, which meant that there were no music jobs or an occasional gig here and there. I had to get a factory job, a truck driving job, a construction job. So I did that every year except for my last year. When I went my last year I said you know what? I’m going to stay in Boston and see what I can pick up. And I stayed in town and as soon as — like a week afterwards I got a call to do a summer in Old Orchard Beach, Maine. It was a quartet. Gene Roma, the drummer, a very fine drummer, was in the band. And I went up there and did that for about two months, or a month and a half, and then my brother Joe was working with Chuck Israels and Hod O’Brien down in Tanglewood. And he said, you know there’s a jazz club here across the street up on the hill called Avalock, which they have a jazz club in there and Randy Weston is leaving and they’re looking for — they put a — you ever see that movie “The Gig?” where they’ve got all these guys — well this was the gig. Exactly like it. They put all these guys together, young college guys had gotten this gig and they needed a saxophone player. So my brother Joe finagled it and I left the gig in Old Orchard Beach, came down to Tanglewood and took this gig and it was all of us living in a house. Now they didn’t have a drummer so they ended up getting the guy who was the bass player, the real jazz guy in the movie, they ended up getting a drummer actually who was the real jazz guy. Gene Gammage was the drummer that worked with Oscar Peterson, Chet Baker, Zoot Sims, and Gene was looking for a gig. So he came up. And so here’s all of these young college guys and this one guy who’d been on the road with everybody and lived with Scott LaFaro and lived with Joe Romano. So Gene, of course he’s — I got to hang out with him and he became a real close friend all through the years. And then I went back to Berklee and that was my last year. I started the semester in September, about two weeks in — you want me to keep going with this story because this is where it goes.
Yeah, yeah.

Okay so I went back to Berklee. Jimmy Mosher was the alto player who had just gotten off the summer tour with Buddy Rich. He did the “Away We Go” Jackie Gleason special, but he came back to Berklee to teach. So they put me in his ensemble, and I was in for about two weeks. On the second week we all go to a bar afterwards on a Friday night rehearsal — me, Lynn Bivvy — well Lynn had left already. And Lynn had gone on the © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

road — Lynn Biviano, the trumpet player. And he was out with Woody Herman. And so Jimmy Mosher was hanging out with Johnny in the bar and he said, “You know you’ve been in school too long.” He said, “You should go out on the road.” And we’re all drinking. And he said, “There’s a job opening with Buddy Rich. I’m going to make a call and get you the gig.” This was while we’re all drinking on Friday. So Monday morning comes around and I see Jimmy Mosher and I say, “Okay where’s that gig with Buddy Rich?” He said, “Quit all your classes and leave for New York, you start Thursday.” So I said oh my God. And I was in the recording band with Herb — I had to go tell Herb Pomeroy I was leaving school. I had to fly home and get a suitcase and I’d never flown before. I had to go back to Rochester. I had to fly to New York, and Ernie Watts, Ernie and I were already in an ensemble the year before with Charlie Mariano, but Ernie had taken the gig with Buddy Rich playing lead alto. And Charlie Owens, who was in Berklee also had taken the second alto gig. So when Jimmy Mosher got me the gig Ernie knew who I was, cause we had worked together. So I went to New York and I rehearsed for a week with the band without playing. We were working The Riverboat and I went down every night and caught the band so I could see what was going on. Last night Bobby Keller was the saxophone player, he came up to me and handed me the bag of suits, because there was a suit and a tuxedo. He says, “You got it.” Sunday morning we flew to Minneapolis/St. Paul. The first night, Frank Sinatra. At first, I get off the bus and Jay Corre, who was the tenor player, missed the plane, so I had to play the lead book, which I had never seen. I had only been rehearsing the fourth book. Now I’m stuck playing “West Side Story” and then backing Sinatra. A test of fire.
You can’t make this up.
No. The thing is, both of my gigs, when I went with Elvin it was the same thing. No preparation just like bang, just jump in there and had to do it.
Well that’s like graduate school, you know? You can only learn so much in school. What was Buddy like to play right in the beginning for? Was he like —

You know he hardly, he just said hello to me at the airport, and you know I could see the show business aspect of it, because he would always, Buddy was Buddy. And I just kept my head low and just read the book, did the book. Jay Corre came back after a couple of nights and I went back to the fourth book. And we were just touring around. We did one month’s tour down into the south. We went back to Los Angeles and played Marty’s on the Hill I believe, and then we left for a tour of the Orient. We went to Taipei and Hong Kong and Japan, and all through, and then ended up in Hawaii. So we did a month tour into the whole month of December into January.
Was your mother happy for you? © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

I think they missed the fact that I wasn’t there for Christmas the first year of ’67 — I was Christmas in Japan. You know that was hard for an Italian family, not having everybody together. And then, they both were, my father was, I mean the first time he saw me on the “Ed Sullivan Show” he goes everything looks fine you know.

That’s great. Well moving from any big band, as you mentioned, you get a limited amount of time to solo. You know sometimes the leader might say open it up, go around again, but still not too long. So going to Elvin Jones, I’m guessing that was a big change in adjustment for you.

Yeah we used to have a chart on Buddy’s band called “Uptight.” Do you remember that? [sings] Uptight. So Dave Liebman told me he says, “Man you went from uptight to up loose” you know. Because you know all of a sudden now I’m coming from, you know, you have a solo in a big band and you stand up, you’ve got to go, it’s like machine gun time you know, most of the time, unless it’s a ballad or a medium thing, but you have to kind of jump in there. And you don’t leave space, none of that stuff really comes — now I go with Elvin, the only thing he ever told me, a couple of things was I played the Vanguard and he said, “Look, you’re not playing long enough.” Because we only played four tunes a set, maybe five. Four tunes a set. So he says, “And you’ve got to take your time and develop your solo.” And that’s something that I had learned earlier on from Lester Young. So it wasn’t hard to go back to it, but you know don’t forget I had almost done seven years with Buddy Rich of doing the other thing. Now I have to go back and learn a whole new way of playing. Because with Buddy I was always playing on top of the beat. Now Elvin’s time was really — there was a lot of space in the bar that Elvin has, a lot of space. Joe Farrell told me, he said, “Once you play with Elvin,” he said, “you’ll have the — you’ll realize what your time is and you’ll have the best time that you could ever think about.” Because he’s not going to spoon feed you. It’s not [claps] it’s like a big wash of sound. And you had to kind of learn how to put — put your lines on top of it, not rush, be relaxed, take your time, leave space, leave space to draw the rhythm section into your solo, which again was something I had learned from Lester Young.
Was the difference in bass players — make a difference in your playing when you were with Elvin?

Yeah. Because the bass player a lot of times, you would rely on the bass player to kind of give you the steady four, where Elvin would kind of maybe — playing loosey goosey around it. Strong bass players — you know Elvin relied on a strong bass player. He didn’t like a bass player that played the amp over the sound of the string — you know the percussiveness of the string. You know if he was putting this much intensity into the ride cymbal, and the bass player was just doing this because he’s allowing it, there’s a mismatch of energy that isn’t there. And he would feel it. So he would get really upset at © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-
that. He didn’t have many of those guys. All the guys that I played with, from when I first went on, were all strong bass players.
I don’t know if you can answer this but if you were playing an extended solo with Elvin Jones’ trio, what is going through your head? Are you thinking harmonically? That’s my question.

No I know all the changes. When I learn a tune I have to know everything that’s going on that there needs to be. Do I hear it at first? Maybe not. When I first learned how to memorize in blocks, when I was working in the factories, that’s how I learned my tunes. I used to work for Mohawk Tires and I worked for the canning factory in Mount Morris where I had to load pallets, stack pallets up with boxes six feet high and then ring the buzzer for the forklift, and the next stack. So I’d do this all day long. So I would bring my tune in, and I had a tune on an index card with the changes all written out. And I’d tack it up to the post that was right next to me, and as the boxes came down I’m going G minor seventh, C minor seventh. And by the time I got home at night I knew the changes like I learned poetry. Because I had a great English teacher who taught me how to memorize poems. And so I learned them. But I didn’t hear them. Now I get home, I know all the changes and don’t have to look at a book. I know the melody and now I start looking at the melody and seeing what I memorized, and then starting to play up and down what I had memorized to hear it that way. So it’s kind of a weird way of learning how to play, but that’s how I did it. So when I was with Elvin, the changes were not a problem. Then I realized that melody is really your prime source to glean improvisational ideas from. My biggest thing is, listen to somebody play “Straight No Chaser.” Okay? You got that melody [scats] all that chromaticism. The minute the head stops, how many people reference the melody? They go right into their stock way of playing on the blues, but yet there’s that great source there of all that chromatic material. Very few people glean — and that’s a good way to practice. Think of that tune and then solo off that tune, and then go back to playing standard and think about well what does that melody mean?
Good advice.

I mean today, I mean a lot of it is technique. There’s so much technique involved in playing today. You know Bobby Shew once told me a great — you know Bobby Shew — he told me a great statement that I’ve always remembered. He said, “Do you play to impress or do you play to inspire?” And so I always think about that when I play. I’m not trying to dazzle you with my technique. I’m trying to like draw you into a theme, a melody, a theme, a set of changes in a direction that I’m going with my solo. So building the solo is important you know. I think you have to depend on who just soloed before you, because you have to keep that in your mind. If you have somebody playing hundreds of notes and a really busy solo, you can’t come in and keep doing that because it’s going © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-
to just be a continuation — and if you want people to listen to you basically you have to deflect the direction and go a different way to build your solo, to grab the listener.

If you’re teaching a student and they are, let’s supposed they’re playing on “So What.” And they’re obviously missing the half-step change. My question is about wrong notes. What term do you use with them with — I mean wrong notes now seems to be a thing like well don’t call them wrong notes. So how do you approach them with — you’re playing wrong notes. That’s the best I can say.

Yeah what I do is I actually make students play wrong notes. I’ll do a tune like “So What” and I’ll just say okay, let’s figure out the notes that are going to sound bad on D minor seventh, okay? Let’s figure the notes that are going to be something, and let’s work on hitting that note. E flat. Right? Okay, and F sharp on the D minor seven chord. Let’s practice hitting those notes, first of all to get rid of the fear of hitting a wrong note. Because that’s one thing that keeps people from going, keeps them from searching, is they’re always afraid like oops I’m going to — so I just say, “Okay let’s play a blues.” I play a blues and I say, “Just play as much activity that you want that is chromatic and out but resolve it toward the end, come back into the chord.” So if you’ve got D minor seventh, play three bars out of chromatic nonsense no matter what you hear but get into the D minor back at the end. Now hold some of those notes that you find unpleasant and resolve them. See where they go, so that if you’re ever into that spot where — but don’t be afraid of them. Because those sometimes are the strengthening notes that pull you into the chord some — you know upper and lower — well I don’t want to get too technical, but upper and lower — appoggiatura — upper and lower chord tones, half step above, half step below, pentatonics. I do that all the time with the students. If I have them playing on a D minor pentatonic I’ll say, okay play the pentatonic a flat six away and a flat five — or you know a sharp five and a flat five away. So D minor right, with the B flat minor pentatonic, play a couple of notes of B flat minor, come into D minor. More notes of B flat minor, come back in. Do the same thing — it’s the root and the fifth, right? Because in harmony the fifth can always be replaced by another note. The root has to be there but the fifth is one of the notes that you can kind of get rid of on a chord and still keep the quality, right? So this is a device to train you. So D minor seventh, you would play E flat minor pentatonic, right, or a C sharp minor into D, right? Or a half step above the fifth, B flat minor or A flat minor below the fifth. But you just play a few of those notes and then come back in. And then a few notes out and then come back. Just get used to hearing those notes out but feel the resolution. That’s a little more advanced than learning how to play one or two wrong notes, but those are devices that you can use because if you hear anybody play “So What” nobody plays in the mode at all. Maybe Miles’ first solo he stayed pretty strict into the D minor, but then after that everybody © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

went out, in and out of the chord, up or low, the neighbor tones, there’s so many devices, with Trane it was superimposed “Giant Steps” changes over it before he would come back in. But there was so much theory there, but it all came from the fact that if you want to play the Dorian mode in a church setting the way those church modes, fine. You stay in the mode in a traditional way of speaking. But nobody ever plays that way when you’re playing.

That’s very interesting because we make such a big deal out of modes. But I’m not sure that the people that are making a big deal about it are actually players. Sometimes they are critics trying to figure out how to describe —

I mean what we learn as modes, I mean everybody’s been playing those for centuries and improvising on them too you know. It gets a little bit hairier if you go on to more advanced thinking like Messian, you know Messian the composer, his modes of limited transposition take you in another direction, they’re a whole different way of thinking about music. You know the altered scales and the diminished scales and all those things, the pentatonic scales and the Hungarian double harmonics and all of these scales — people use them in jazz but —
Well you went from Woody Herman and Buddy Rich and Elvin Jones, were there any gigs that you turned down along the way?

Well I was with Woody Herman only for a short bit, I just went out to help Frank Tiberi and they just called me up as a sub. I loved it, but I wasn’t with them for a long time. Same with the Glenn Miller band. I went out for a bit to help somebody that needed to get off for a week. Yeah, I turned down Joe Henderson believe it or not, I’ll tell you why, because I was studying with Joe Henderson in New York. I was on Buddy Rich’s band. And you know Joe called me one day, I was in a hotel, the President Hotel in New York and he called me and he said, “I need somebody to go on, to play bass clarinet.” He wanted me to play bass clarinet. I said, “Joe, I can’t play bass clarinet.” I think Pete Yellin was doing the gig maybe at the time. I’m not sure if Pete was doing it. But he wanted me to go out and play with the band and he had this idea of bass clarinet and I just said I can’t do it. I’m not a bass clarinet player. I mean I had to play clarinet with Buddy’s band and I started on that instrument, but no way was I going to go out and embarrass myself with Joe Henderson.
He had a big band at the time?

This was the small band. He had like I think it was either Julian Priester, or I think he had three horns in front. I know at one point he had alto, trombone and himself on tenor. I had seen that band at the Vanguard. I don’t know what he was thinking at the time, but he was always composing. When I was with him he was writing for Blood, Sweat & Tears, © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-
when I was studying with him he was kind of doing that Blood, Sweat & Tears band that never took off. They were just rehearsing all the time.
I remember seeing that, like Joe Henderson is with Blood, Sweat & Tears? Because I loved Blood, Sweat & Tears.

I went to take a lesson one time and Joe says, “Look at this,” he said, “I got a complete brand new Magnavox sound system.” He goes, “They gave me a tenor, a bari, an alto, a soprano.” Because Magnavox owned Selmer at the time. He said, “I got all of this stuff they gave me because I joined a rock band. I played jazz all my life nobody ever gave me anything,” he said, “I go with one rock band and look at all the stuff they give me.”
Going back to Buddy for a minute, of course it was mostly young guys but there was some older veterans in that band like Al Porcino.
Yeah, Al came on just after I joined. He came on in January of ’68.
Were those guys, did they teach you anything?

Yeah I mean Al Porcino and Art Pepper came on right at the same time, right? So I sat next to Art Pepper for almost a year on Buddy’s band, and Menza came on around the same time too. See when Jay Corre left in Vegas in ’68 I took the tenor chair for about a month and then Don Menza came on the lead chair and I went back to the fourth chair, which was good for me because I got a chance to kind of hang out with Art Pepper and hang out with Don, who taught me a lot. Menza taught me a lot. I mean he was like a father to me, he taught me all kinds of — still to this day we talk almost every week. And so yeah, I’d hang out with these guys, Art Pepper was great. Al was really interesting, and he had given me a whole bunch of Charlie Parker tapes. I used to drive him around. I had a Volkswagen that I rented and I would take him to places that he had to go. And he gave me a bunch of Charlie Parker reel to reel tapes that he had done when he was on Woody’s band and he had played the Apollo Theater and he took his reel to reel tape recorder and held it up backstage next to the speaker back there, and he taped all of these Bird shows and then he gave them to me and I put them on cassette. I still have them downstairs. They’re all out on CD now but, yeah Al would give me stuff. And of course a lot of stories about all those, the older guys.
Yeah. I heard a story, something about the Playboy Club with Buddy Rich and Al?

Yeah downstairs in Hugh Hefner’s, he had a game room downstairs in the bar with a big glass window that went into the swimming pool. And Al Porcino swam by with nothing on, in the nude, by the window of the pool. Yeah.
Did your, your entrance into jazz education and academia, was that partly to change a lifestyle of being on the road?

Teacher’s College and never thought about teaching. Went to Berklee, it never crossed my mind. I moved to Canada in ’74 and I was with Yamaha at the time. I had signed with Yamaha in the States, the last couple of months with Buddy Rich and so when I came to Canada I was with Yamaha. And they called me and they said we’ve got this young student who is, they called him the “rising star” the Yamaha Rising Star Award. And we wondered if you’d give him a couple of lessons. I said gee, I never taught anybody. I don’t know about teaching. They said well give him a try. So I had him come by my house on Saturday mornings, and we’d go there for four hours, and I’d basically just retraced my steps of how I learned, what I did. Because I had lots of notes. I mean I had been, since being at Berklee I had all kinds of notes. I learned how to take notes. I learned how to write all my practice routines down. So I just — I listened to him play and I could see what he needed, if it was musculature, embouchure, whatever, I could see that. And then the theory about improvisation was something I had just picked up on my own through a Berklee correspondence course when I was in Potsdam I was studying the Berklee correspondence course. And all the stuff I had learned at Berklee and then with Herb Pomeroy and Ray Santisi, Charlie Mariano, basically I just retraced my steps and showed him what to do. And then there was a college here in Toronto called Humber. Humber College is the Berklee of Canada. They had the first program. Matter of fact some of the guys from Berklee came up to help them establish this school. And there was an arranger named Ron Collier, one of Canada’s most famous arrangers, one of the only guys that ever arranged for Duke Ellington and write for Duke Ellington in Canada. He started this program at Humber and they had been running about three or four years and they heard that I had taught this kid, who went eventually to this school. And they called me and asked me, they said, “Would you like to teach three more students?” I said, okay, private lessons and I wasn’t getting a lot of work. See when I first moved to Canada I couldn’t work for six months because of the union rules. You know they had a rule you couldn’t work a steady job. I was sneaking across the borders, before computers and they could check up on you, I would go back to Rochester to work Italian weddings. I’d work up north so they couldn’t trace me. You had to kind of do everything under the table. Because you weren’t allowed to work a steady gig. I had a baby on the way and so I couldn’t do it. So I took this job, and then Elvin called me in ’75, like a year later I got the call and he had been trying to get me because he because he wanted me to join, he sat in once in Buddy’s band in Ronnie Scott’s a year before. He came in and sat in and took my number to see if I was interested. But then I moved to Canada and he lost all my contact information. So he called me. And that was around 1975. So taking this part time job teaching and then Elvin called me. So I took the job with Jones and I did the part time lessons as I could throughout the semester, which was something they allowed me to do. © Fillius Jazz Archive -15-

I said, you know I’m going to be, I’ve got to travel to make a living here because I’m not doing anything in town. And so that’s what happened. I got the job with Elvin and then I started to get more and more students each year but it was always part time until the 80s when they offered me a — in ’87 they offered me a full time position. So I was off and on with Elvin for almost twenty years plus. I would go out with him — ’75, ’76, ’77, ’78, ’79 — I was with him pretty much. Then I left for a bit, came back, left, came back, helped him out. And then his last two years I went back for his 75th birthday tour and did two years on a sabbatical that I had taken from the school, and then he passed away in the following year.

This was when, we went down for the CIA it was like a branch of the CIA called the US Information Service. They sent us to every trouble spot in South America, right? So we went to Uruguay, Paraguay, Chile, Medellin, Bogota, Guayaquil, Santiago. You know, every place where there was some — they sent us down as kind of a peace thing. So we went there with that. We went to Japan with Elvin. In the states we always had a circuit. We would work the Vanguard two or three times a year. We worked a jazz showcase in Chicago. I don’t remember — we worked a couple of other places in Detroit, Baker’s Keyboard Lounge. There were some other spotty places that we would work but that’s about it. There were only a few places. I don’t remember — California we’d work the Jazz Bakery. But there wasn’t a lot of activity going on at that time.

But you know what? Working with my father as a kid, learning how to work firemen’s picnics and clam bakes and weddings and all of these jobs where you just took them because it was work, I just learned how to tough it out and tough it through. that it was always going to get better, there was always going to be bad nights and it’s just one of those things. There’s always good nights coming down the road at some point, you hope.

One Suite” goes [counts quickly], so it had that kind of, you know that fake three and five, which is really eight. But you know that’s the way it was broken up. He listened to it for just a little bit and then he went, “Get off the drums” and he went up and played the part.

Yeah. Menza on that.

when I first moved here I was really upset about the fact that my taxes all of a sudden, whoa, why am I paying this amount of taxes. Guys that can afford it then so what, and then everybody’s covered. I’m telling you, I think that would make a lot of things better down there. I feel, I don’t know, you know you have a teaching job you get it. But if you work with certain companies you have a medical plan. But if you get fired or laid off it’s gone, a lot of it.
All right. I appreciate the observation. Do you have any personal feelings about why this pandemic has occurred? Why it occurred in 2019?

I don’t. I mean I just know that this is something that’s been coming. My outlook on this right now is I’m trying not to be negative. I try to use this time for myself to grow. I’m exercising, I’m practicing every day, exercising, trying to get out. Luckily now I have a house with a backyard and different rooms and different levels that I can go to. If I had an apartment I may be thinking differently. But you can still use it as a period for growth. I’ve always been — that was my thought all the time. I’m always thinking ahead and planning for the next thing to come and being ready for it. So I think you can use this time to kind of be ready for what’s to come. I don’t know why, I just know that when I was a kid, when I grew up, my mother had to wear masks. My mother would come home © Fillius Jazz Archive -22-

at night and she’d have to take her clothes off on the porch and hang them outside, and come in and take a shower. She worked with tuberculosis patients. So from a young kid all the way on, we were dealing with this all the time, with this, you don’t want to catch this. Then all of a sudden polio kicks in and we had to deal with polio. So you probably were around at that time.
Yes.
So we all know — I remember my mother had to wear the masks all the time on the wards.
All right. Well Pat this has really been great. And I’m glad we connected.

Yeah, Monk, thank you very much. I hope this helps you and if you need anything else from me — now I’ll try to get these done today, I’ll see if I can remember how to fill out a W-2 or whatever they call it.
Okay. I’m going to pause our recording and then we can sort of say adios.
Sure. © Fillius Jazz Archive -23-

segments.title: Opening and introductions for the Hamilton interview
segments.summary: Boilerplate, and Monk Rowe welcomes Pat LaBarbera to the Zoom interview.

segments.title: The LaBarbera family band in Mount Morris
segments.summary: Local newspapers covered the family band; his father got the boys going and his mother learned bass to join.

segments.title: Early paid gigs and the family band repertoire
segments.summary: They earned about five dollars a wedding in 1954-55; the book was swing, stock arrangements, Italian tunes and transcribed solos.

segments.title: First time improvising at a Dansville talent contest
segments.summary: He lost his place reading a written solo, improvised, and loved it; a school teacher later sparked his jazz interest.

segments.title: Local notoriety and the Mickey Mouse Club audition
segments.summary: The brothers got newspaper articles and auditioned for Ted Mack and the Mickey Mouse Club in Rochester, where Steve Gadd also auditioned.

segments.title: Getting along with his brothers
segments.summary: No rivalry; he brought John and Joe into jazz and their father made sure there were no grudges.

segments.title: Turned down at Fredonia, studying saxophone at Potsdam
segments.summary: Rejected at Fredonia for sight singing, he became the first saxophone-only student at Potsdam in 1962 and clashed with Musser and his clarinet teacher.

segments.title: Describing his own playing and early influences
segments.summary: Prez, Getz, Mulligan, Rollins, Coltrane and Johnny Hodges shaped his sound.

segments.title: Grove's Coltrane comparison and recognition with Elvin
segments.summary: Early Trane contains Prez, Ammons and Dexter; he was noticed as a soloist with Elvin more than in Buddy's big band.

segments.title: Hearing Coltrane live and in the daytime at the Jazz Workshop
segments.summary: He heard Coltrane in 1964-66 and, while at Berklee, watched him practice at the Jazz Workshop.

segments.title: What he copied from Coltrane
segments.summary: He studied Trane's sound, vibrato and solos, and his later albums.

segments.title: Paying for Berklee and his brothers following
segments.summary: He worked a year for tuition; his father borrowed from shady lenders, and John and Joe later came to Berklee.

segments.title: Berklee years and summer gigs in Maine and Tanglewood
segments.summary: He learned everything at Berklee, took summer work in Old Orchard Beach, then a Tanglewood-area jazz club gig through Joe.

segments.title: Getting the Buddy Rich job through Jimmy Mosher
segments.summary: Mosher got him the Buddy Rich gig; he left school in days and first played lead book for Sinatra.

segments.title: First weeks and Far East tour with Buddy Rich
segments.summary: Buddy barely spoke; they toured the South, Los Angeles, Asia and Hawaii over Christmas 1967.

segments.title: From Buddy's big band to Elvin's open space
segments.summary: Going from Uptight to up loose, he had to take time, leave space and play behind the beat.

segments.title: Elvin Jones and strong bass players
segments.summary: Elvin needed strong bassists who matched his intensity.

segments.title: Memorizing changes in the factory and using melody
segments.summary: He learned changes on index cards at factory jobs and advises soloists to draw on the melody.

segments.title: Playing to inspire and building a solo
segments.summary: Bobby Shew's advice and thoughts on shaping a solo against the previous soloist.

segments.title: Teaching students to play wrong notes and modes
segments.summary: He has students practice outside notes on So What and discusses how modes are really used.

segments.title: Turning down Joe Henderson
segments.summary: Short stints with Herman and Miller; he refused Henderson's bass clarinet job, and recalls Henderson's rock band gear.

segments.title: Veterans in Buddy's band: Porcino, Pepper and Menza
segments.summary: He sat by Art Pepper, learned from Menza, and Al Porcino gave him Parker tapes and swam nude at the Playboy Club.

segments.title: Moving to Canada, starting to teach and joining Elvin
segments.summary: He began teaching in Toronto at Yamaha's request, moved to Canada in 1974, then Elvin called him in 1975.

segments.title: Touring with Elvin in Europe, South America and the US
segments.summary: Mostly Europe, a US Information Service tour of South America, Japan and a few US clubs.

segments.title: Race on the bandstand and on the road
segments.summary: Ernie Watts and Charlie Owens could not swim in Florida; Elvin did not see color.

segments.title: Jamey Aebersold camps and letting students create
segments.summary: Everyone can improvise; he taught for Aebersold and at Skidmore.

segments.title: Staying in touch with his brothers and retirement
segments.summary: Weekly Zoom with John and Joe; his retirement plans during Covid.

segments.title: Declining to repeat a Tony Bennett and Hibbler story
segments.summary: He declines to tell a story he only heard secondhand.

segments.title: Terrible gigs and toughing it out
segments.summary: A barnyard costume gig after the Vanguard, and how the family jobs taught him endurance.

segments.title: Why Buddy Rich looked left, and the wristwatch
segments.summary: Buddy watched lead players breathe to anticipate charts, and relied on Pat for timing.

segments.title: Bass players and hiring for Buddy
segments.summary: Buddy had trouble with bassists and Pat hired and fired them.

segments.title: Joel DeBartolo and Give me an A
segments.summary: Buddy collapsed laughing when nervous bassist Joel answered his tuning gag.

segments.title: Canadian views of America, taxes and health care
segments.summary: He talks politics and describes Canadian health coverage and Covid subsidies.

segments.title: The pandemic and his mother's tuberculosis ward
segments.summary: He uses lockdown for growth and recalls his mother nursing tuberculosis patients.

segments.title: Closing thanks
segments.summary: Goodbyes and a paperwork joke.
